A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GameFactory and GF-Minecraft. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original action-control ablations in Table 1, scene-generalization experiments in Appendix B and Table 3, and generated-video examples.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original dataset comparisons, action-frequency analysis and an autoregressive loss-scope ablation in Tables 4–6.

M1.justification: The domain adapter in v2 is the existing LoRA component: learn game style, freeze it while training action control, then remove it for open-domain inference. Keyboard cross-attention, mouse concatenation, action grouping and autoregressive training on predicted frames remain unchanged. The new loss-scope ablation evaluates the existing procedure.

E1.justification: v2 newly uses human-gameplay clips from VPT's Find Cave dataset to train a comparison model (Section 6.4). This extends data coverage within Minecraft; GF-Minecraft, open-domain scenes, racing examples and the action-controlled generation tasks are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds two focused comparators: a VPT-trained model in Table 4 and an all-frame-loss variant in Table 6. Existing action-injection and one-phase versus multi-phase comparisons remain. The other game engines in new Table 1 are descriptive comparisons, not newly evaluated head-to-head baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds GLOMAP-based camera-pose error and FVD to the existing evaluations, and introduces training-data and autoregressive loss-scope comparison protocols. The reported 5% holdout, three action subsets, backbone and training budgets remain unchanged. Flow, CLIP and Dom rename existing metrics rather than introducing different measurements.

E4.justification: New analyses test the benefit of balanced training actions through dataset comparison, action frequencies and backward-movement/jumping failure cases (Tables 4–5, Figure 9). Table 6 newly tests whether autoregressive loss should include history frames. The earlier action-injection and multi-phase ablations remain; collision and racing cases are relocated to Appendix B.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, error bars or significance tests. Both present point estimates; the additional metrics and results do not change uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: All shared scores in v1 Tables 1 and 3 are retained, while v2 adds Cam/FVD scores and dataset, action-frequency and long-video results. New Table 4 reports Flow of 43.48 for GF-Minecraft versus 107.67 for VPT, but CLIP of 0.3135 versus 0.3174. Table 6 reports FVD of 1154.45 for predicted-frame-only loss versus 1592.43 for all-frame loss. Figure 10 shows a rollout through frame 326.

T1.justification: v2 omits the explicit Gaussian forward-noising formula and separate text-only denoising objective from v1 Equations 1–2. The action-conditioned objective and action-grouping/fusion relationships remain, largely with inline notation. This is a limited reduction in formal preliminaries; neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows v1's blanket statement that existing methods fail to address scene generalization to 'most existing methods' in v2. The substantive contributions—scene-generalizable action control, GF-Minecraft, style-action decoupling and unlimited-length autoregressive generation—remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation that predicted-frame-only loss avoids irrelevant noise interference from history frames, and discusses obstacles to unified benchmarking across game engines. It removes v1 Appendix B.1's qualification that mouse-control variants were difficult to distinguish visually. Existing first-person applicability and long-memory/real-time limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 identifies GLOMAP for pose extraction, describes VPT Find Cave selection and updates the printed project/dataset address. It omits v1's conditional-frame noise setting of 15/1000 and the fuller scene-generalization evaluation recipe; continued use of that noise setting is unspecified. Backbone, hardware, LoRA hyperparameters and Appendix A preprocessing details remain.

R1.justification: v2 expands coverage of earlier game-generation research, including GameGAN, DriveGAN and playable/promptable models, while removing three next-token-video references. New Table 1 systematically positions competing engines by capabilities and resources. The discussion acknowledges Genie 2 and Matrix's generalization progress and emphasizes GameFactory's complex action space and broader demonstrated testing.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. The former Method section becomes separate preliminaries, action-controlled generation and scene-generalization sections, with autoregression moved earlier. Appendix comparisons move into the main experiments, while collision, racing and world-model discussion move into appendices. Mathematical exposition is also substantially condensed.

P2.justification: The architecture figure is split into Figures 3–4, and earlier appendix comparisons are resized and moved into main-text Figures 7–8. The old standalone style-bias and atomic-action displays are removed. New comparison tables and dataset/long-video figures are added, existing tables gain metric columns, and collision/racing displays are rearranged in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens support for the dataset and autoregressive design through the new VPT comparison and loss-scope ablation, while Cam/FVD broaden existing evaluations. The central scene-generalization comparison already existed in v1 Appendix B. These gains are limited by unspecified sample/budget matching for VPT and the loss of conditional-noise and scene-evaluation details, yielding a modest net improvement.
